projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Jack Stout was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran Jack A. Stout. Mr. Stout served in the U.S. Navy in the Pacific Theater. I am Tom Swope and this interview was recorded on the telephone. Mr. Stout called from his home in Granberry, Texas, on January 2, 2003. Jack was 81 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you go into the service?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: I went in October 2, 1940.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What can you tell me about your training?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: My training?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Well, I was in boot camp. And, actually, it started off pretty good in the camp. It wasn't bad. The food was wholesome and all that. But we had an instructor that was a -- really pulled a neat one on us one night. Class had already gone out and we -- all of a sudden somebody was waking us up and it was him shouting. Everybody get your clothes on and come outside. And he cut the clothesline down. He found one pair of dirty skivvies. So he cut them all down and had us march over. Not one guy, all of us marched over. Back and forth. And then we had to wash them and hang them back up before we were allowed to go back to bed.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, where did you take your training?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: San Diego.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: San Diego.

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else you can tell me about those days, your training days?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Well, let's see. I don't guess there was anything in particular. When I went in is when you are talking about?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. Exactly.

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Yeah, there is one thing in particular. (Laughter.) I was the only sailor that had brown shoes. They didn't have any size 14 shoes and I stood out like a sore thumb, of course. And I wore those right until I went aboard ship in 19, late November 1940.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So late November '40, you was assigned to the Saratoga?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Yes, sir.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was life like on the Saratoga?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Saratoga. It was nice. They had real good wholesome food. It was so big that you could just get lost in it real easy. One thing about it when we left boot camp we went to Long Beach on a tankard and got on the Sara the next day and some real high swells came in. They were anchored out. And, it seemed like every time we turned around there would be -- there would be -- they would feed you pork chops. It just seemed like it was for recruits. So I got seasick. And I wasn't the only one. Anyway, the greasier the food seemed like the more we got sick. So what happened was -- I said, oh, my God, just dealing with this thing. I hadn't even gone to sea yet, but I never got seasick again.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So very good. So December 15th is when you got to Hawaii; is that right?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: December 15th, in '41.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what was Pearl Harbor like? And that was a little over a week later. What was it like?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Well, actually, every now and then they would stop hammering and that meant everybody had to shut off. They blew a whistle. There was loud steam horn and fog horn for everybody to stop working. People, And you could see people laying over their hulls listening for anybody that might be tapping. Far as I know they didn't never get anymore out alive. But see all those ships there was, it was undescribable (ph)..

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So how long were you stationed at Honolulu before you went back out to sea?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: We were only there about maybe three or four days and we got -- that's when we finally got our first torpedo. It was about 420 miles from Hawaii. And like I said in my diary, told my dad. We got torpedoed like I said on the 11th of January so I just carried the diary all the way through.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And you say that was about what, 400 miles from Hawaii?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Yeah, about 400 miles. It was merely to mid-way when we got the torpedo.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what was that like? Can you describe when you were torpedoed?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Sure can. I was the gun captain on the fort barrel. And the gun captains, they wore headsets. The big one. A big helmet. So a light flashed and it was a destroyer trying to tell us that the torpedo was coming our way. And about that time somebody on the crows' nest said, torpedo coming. Fort beam. I said, repeat. They said torpedo coming on the fort beam and I just told the guys to hunker down and hang on. Then it hit. The Sara was so big it only had one rutter. I think these modern ships all have two rutters. And we couldn't turn fast. You know they like to head them into the torpedo coming if they can. It was a 105 feet wide but she was 916 feet long.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what did it feel like when it hit?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Well, it hit right square in the middle. I guess it was the worst place to hit. It seemed like it shook -- it seemed like it shook two or three feet or more. So the torpedo was set so low where it wouldn't hit us, destroy our cruiser of ours, so it hit down low and actually it only killed six people that were going down in the hangar deck. And watching them take the scissors and cut that oil and stuff off of them. And that was before we got to Pearl Harbor. Actually, we lifted over to the left about five or six degrees and then it hit what we called a peak tank and that threw in water on the right side and we never did lose any speed. We just kept making 18 knots.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you then headed back for Hawaii, is that right?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: We pulled into Hawaii and just for a few days and then we went on to Birmington, Washington shipyard.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And how long were you in Birmington then?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Oh, we was there for quite a while. It seemed like it was maybe June or July before we got back into the city. One thing when the war broke out, we had three inches of surface on that thing. Saratoga was a battle cruiser originally. A monster of a battle cruiser.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: And, can you imagine a three-inch sail gun used for any of the aircraft so they took that off and gave us a 1.1 and then later we got 40 millimeter.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what happened then after you got back out to sea after repairs?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Well, October 31, we got torpedoed again on the -- side. And the same thing, guys said, torpedo coming, fort beam. Repeat. Torpedo coming, start with beam. This time it was during the daytime. The other it was at dusk and this was at dawn. And one of mysterious deal, I guess, was the planes. We could just picture the enemy planes coming over, you know. We were dead in the water. And it knocked our generators out. And so nothing happened except it was a recruiter came alongside and he towed us for a while. And then when he got near -- Islands, a little bitty tug; I called it little bitty. It was about six feet long. It came out and towed us though. Towed us into -- and on that one we thought well, here we go back to the states. Well, all they did was put a heavy list on the port side and that brought the stronger side up. And the welder just welded. It looked like one inch plate, looked like one inch holes in it. And so it went to a hurdle on the way back to Pearl. Meanwhile, since we had the first torpedo, they put in a float and -- that would float it. So we never got past Pearl on that second one. We thought we was going back to the States.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So then how long were you back in Hawaii?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Not too long. I don't remember the time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you experience much in Honolulu at that time? What was it like there after Pearl Harbor during the war?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Well, it just seemed kind of long to me. I remember the submarine crews. They got a -- the main -- the main hotel on the beach was all reserved for submariners. And it too me just seemed long, you know in August.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Are you still there?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So were they still mistrusting the Japanese-Americans in Hawaii at that point?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: I don't think so in August.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: By then they realized that they weren't as much of a threat?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: No, I really couldn't tell any difference, myself. Aurora, Hawaii was the main.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Exactly, yes. So then it was back out to sea after a while?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Yeah. Back out to sea and I stayed on it until February of 1943. And they was building a new ship, a cruiser. They needed new crews. Some handicaps. Some people that weren't -- some people got to have some knowledge to run one so when they shipped me to Boston I got on the USS Boston there and finally they got it commissioned in November, November '43. We went through the canal and back to Asiatic (ph) Southwest Pacific.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What can you tell me about the experiences on that ship?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The experiences on that ship. Any memorable incidents that you recall?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Well, let's see. I guess, yeah. Here, lately, it seems like people been talking about Harry Truman was such a bad president. Well, I tell you what. We bombarded Iwo Jima on July 4th. And they hit it with either bombs or shells. We were shelling ourselves. And they hit it everyday until it landed in February of '45. The marines landed. Okay. That little island Iwo Jima it took two miles, about five miles, ten square miles. Well, it took them what's that, six or seven months just to take that. And then for President Truman dropping the two eight A bombs, we would still be in Japan.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. So there was about you say more than six months of shelling Iwo Jima before they landed?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Shelling and bombing.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow!

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: And then we went into -- when they unofficially declared the war over in February, I mean August 15th, we had an admiral we called Bull Horsely (ph). He passed the word to everybody. Said, if you see any Japanese planes shoot them down in a friendly way. Nobody trusted them yet. We went on and pulled into them and we was right off of them. Got off at Japan when they -- the Missouri where they finally, the Japanese surrender. And right before they got there I remember this real good. We ran out of toilet paper. Freaky. Weird deal there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did he give you any further instructions about what shooting the planes down in a friendly way would be?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Well, he was quite a character. Mr. Bull Horsely. I'm sure he meant it because that's what they did to us at Pearl. And they let us go ashore there afterwards. And we stayed there around to help clean up. And what it amounted to was they had their boats were on rails up in caves. And they had a torpedo head and, of course, a suicide driver and everyone of them had a 32 chilled A engine in it. And can you imagine up -- they would still be fighting trying to get to Holland as big as Japan trying to get to Iwo Jima.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What were the Japanese people like when you went ashore?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Well, they told us to walk in bunches. And, of course, we had never seen nobody go to the bathroom, you know, number two and all of that on the lodge. That was kind of a surprise. But we stayed in bunches. You know, you just didn't trust them. So we did what the captain said; stay in bunches.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That guy didn't have any problems with any of them?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: No, no. I never heard of any.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what can you tell me about buddies you had on either of the ships?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Well, we got all along real good. To kill time and stuff like that we either shot craps or played cribbets. And the rest of the time back in the war zone we had to save our water, fresh water for the boilers. They just give you fresh water. One guy, well, you asked me about my buddies. We all got along real well. You know, we had a few marines aboard and a few blacks and I thought we got along real well.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And were the blacks restricted to being cooks and that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Yeah, mess tenants for the officers. We had a few marine pilots aboard and besides they kind of helped look out for officers too.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you get close to any of the fires?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Well, I tell you I sure did on the Boston.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: I was in charge of the cranes for lifting the storage aboard. I never seen planes when they came in there was a seaplane on each side, pedal boat. They had to come in right over where what we called a cargo net. And I had sailors up ahead and instead of using wrench power, you used man power. Just kind of hold that or let it out more. That pilot come in there and you cut its engine. And then the plane had just set down right there. And we got -- those guys they seemed like they kind of liked the guys that bring in those cranes because there was a ball above the small hood and it weighed over a hundred pounds. Well, when you are trying to bring a board and it's wavy and you had to have a good touch to keep that big ball from coming in there and trying to kill them. When you lower that little one down first and then hook it on. Then you try to not -- you didn't want to jerk them too hard. We never lost any, so they took care of us. They usually give -- I know they gave my crew little stuff, you know. Little bonuses and things like that. I enjoyed that part of it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any buddies while you were out there?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: On the Boston?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: On either ship?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Just those six on the Sara.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You knew those guys?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Sir?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You knew those guys that you lost on the Saratoga?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: They were engineers. They were down below and I was a boss mate which was top side rate. The Boston -- the first ship we hit with the shells, AA shells. I guess they could heard us shouting all over and just knocked the guy in the stand and he came right on down and crashed. That was our first plane shoot down. Most of the time when you were on the cruiser we would try to fly over to the carriers. And when we were on the carriers well, it was obvious that they were after us. So the destroyers and the cruisers would knock down as many as they could before they got to us.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was that like the first time you were under attack? What did you feel?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Well, you know that old saying, "safety in numbers."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: It just -- I think it's something to that. And I heard the saying, "youth make the best soldiers because they ain't got any sense." And then I know I used to -- after I got on the gun, I really prayed that if this war is ever over I would like to live until I'm thirty years old. Maybe have four or five, six years of civilian life. I would be satisfied.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow! Well, you think about that experience during World War II, is there any particularly memorable memory come to mind? A vivid memory?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: At what time?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any particularly vivid memories when you think about that?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: No. I can't -- no. It just seems like it all came together there. I tell you one thing I never lost a drop of blood to the enemy.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay. Did you get a lot of mail from home? What was mail call like?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Mail call was all censored coming or going. That was the only contact we had except when we was on leave. And I went six years in a row without being home on Christmas. When we were on leave, of course, I visited my folks.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you finally get out then?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: November 11th, 1946. When I joined -- the only way you could join was for six years. So my six years was actually up in October the 1st. I got hurt but not hit by the enemy. I got hurt in 1945 when an ammunition can, empty ammunition can of 1.1 cells fell down and popped me on the knee and it just turned me into -- I wanted to get up one day and I couldn't get up. So I went in the hospital in San Diego. And then they didn't know what it was and then he sent me by a hospital train to Norman, Oklahoma. Norman is usually a lot drier. I stayed there five months. They said we want to send you to a dryer climate. And they sent me right back to Long Beach which is 120 miles from San Diego.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what was your reunion with your family finally like when you got back home?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Oh, it was crazy. My dad he -- it was four of us boys. He used to grab us by the arm and shoulder, and he said, there is the front gate anytime you want to leave. That was out the gate you go. So I take him up on that when I went for six years. And my mother she kept -- he was worried to death. He really loved his sons. I'm sure did.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, very good. You think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Yeah, that pretty well covers that part of it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else you want to add?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Well, we pulled some pranks. I don't know if you --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure. Sure. Yes, I would like to hear about that.

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Okay. On the Saratoga. We had a water trough like a horse trough. And this thing ran 24 hours a day. Water came in one end and out the other. And so every now and then you know men, they usually did what you said, but every now and then you would catch some guy goofing off. Now on the very end where the water ran out they had stalls there, but the rest of the place is just open general. And so you catch a guy that's had been goofing off and he be down there maybe reading a funny book or something on that bottom row. So we would tell somebody, you know you have to watch this. So we would get some newspaper or whatever we had to hold. And on the upper end we would throw the papers in the upper end and you could imagine the screams. That was something else. And then there is another one I'd like to mention. When I was on the Boston, we were in the battle zone and we couldn't use any of the fresh water. And so I saw this, we called then 90 day wonders. Anybody who had a profession, it seemed like they gave them officers' jobs. And I saw him go over there and my men were washing down the boathead on the fantail and so this guy went over there and stuck his finger in that water and he said, I'm putting you on report. And, you know, I tried to tell him, no, no. So I didn't have a chance to tell him. So he threw me on report and went up and told the captain. And the captain, said, well, this is going to be a dead (ph) court marshal. I said, what? And I didn't say what, but he said, you got anything to say for yourself. And I said, yes sir. Every three months we -- what they call water breakers on the -- you change them and put fresh water in them. And so instead of just letting that water run down the waterway, I caught it and we were using fresh water. And he chewed -- so that officer he said, the captain said what you got to say for yourself. And I said, I tell you what, I told him just what I was telling you. And he said, well, that's -- I can't believe that you are putting this man on report and all he is trying to do is keep his end of the ship clean. He chewed his butt out good. I can't think of any more pranks.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was the food pretty good on those ships?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: I thought it was pretty wholesome. Only one place it wasn't. Our mess deck was on the second deck down from the plat (ph) deck. And anytime we were near Australia it seemed like they shipped us a lot of lamb mutton. And you could smell that lamb mutton coming up out of those hatches. I mean it -- I like lamb mutton, but I seen 90 percent of sailors wouldn't even go down there to the mess hall when they had lamb mutton. The smell coming out of those hatches there on top side just knock you over. As a whole they had pretty good food. I couldn't eat the powdered eggs or powdered milk. Most of the time you didn't have any choice, you know. Whatever they put on the tray is what you got.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. Yeah. All right. Anything else?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: I can't think of anything. This is really nice of you taking the time to --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: - to get the story from us old guys.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, I loved listening to my dad's stories and I like listening to you guys too.

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: I ended up with 16 battle stars.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow!

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: The Asiatic Pacific Medal, 14 stars, a Philippine Liberation Medal, 2 stars. And later on they added a Japan Occupation Medal which is a red medal, I didn't get it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sound like you were in just about every naval engagement that happened out there.

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: It wasn't but 23 of us.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I think you had 23, I guess. I talked to a guy that was on the Enterprise. I think they were in 20 or 21, something like that.

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Yeah. Well, I remember the Enterprise real good.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: One battle out there I think was that Marijuana (ph).

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mariannas, maybe.

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Yes. And they got hit. We had to take their planes aboard. Of course, we already had planes. And it was the most planes I ever saw in my life. Ever will see. DFW or any other airport. They had to set down the planes by the nearest destroyer because they were running out of fuel. And believe it or not they landed with their wheels down. I didn't quite understand that. And what it did when you drop them in their, you just planted on a carrier, you know. And so we didn't lose any one of those pilots.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow!

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Destroyers picked them up right away.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So they landed in the ocean and you fished them out?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: We didn't but the destroyers did. Picked out of the destroyers.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But the planes were lost, I assume, right?

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, with no rooms to put those in. You couldn't hook those up to the cranes and pull them out. Wow! That's amazing.

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: It was a great six years. I enjoyed it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jack Stout
sp.p: And I'm glad to live through it.
